label: Impulse!
rationale: Karma is the defining statement of spiritual jazz and Sanders' most acclaimed record: 'The Creator Has a Master Plan' extends the A Love Supreme lineage (Sanders was Coltrane's last-band tenor) into a communal, chant-based modal language that became a genre template. Consensus across independent traditions: AllMusic 5 stars, Penguin Guide 3 stars, Pitchfork #53 of the 1960s, Jazzwise '100 Jazz Albums That Shook the World', New Yorker 100 essential jazz albums. Session gravity is high: Lonnie Liston Smith, Leon Thomas, Reggie Workman, Richard Davis, Ron Carter, Billy Hart, Freddie Waits. Admissibility note: Wikipedia tags it free jazz — arrivals from the free-jazz gate lean scope_call/contested per the rubric, but this record's center is a loping modal groove with sung melody, the teaching record for the idiom.

scope_check.boundary_note: The 1969 date is safely in range, but the newly opened free-jazz gate is genuinely in play: sources classify the album as free jazz while its long-form chant, melody, and loping modal groove make it a direct late-Coltrane/modal bridge rather than straightforward energy-music maximalism.

ballot.case_for: Karma is Sanders' defining leader statement and a foundational spiritual-jazz record: "The Creator Has a Master Plan" transforms the devotional modal language of Coltrane's late work into a communal, vocal-led form that became a durable genre template. Its consensus case is unusually broad, with the dossier citing Penguin Guide, AllMusic, Pitchfork's 1960s ranking, Jazzwise's "100 Jazz Albums That Shook the World," and the New Yorker's essential-albums list. Sanders' direct late-Coltrane lineage, Leon Thomas's singular vocal presence, and the session's network—Lonnie Liston Smith, Reggie Workman, Richard Davis, Ron Carter, Billy Hart, and Freddie Waits—make it both a load-bearing bridge and an unusually accessible teaching record for spiritual jazz.
ballot.case_against: The record's ecstatic tenor language, overblowing, and open-ended chant format can place it on the free-jazz side of the canon's center of gravity, directly testing John's stated difficulty with that idiom even though the underlying pulse is modal. The dossier also falls short of the preferred research standard: its substantive personnel and recording claims rest chiefly on Wikipedia (S1), while three listed sources are identifier or cover-art services, and several track assignments—including Workman, Watkins, and part two of the title piece—are inferred rather than confirmed.
ballot.disagreement: Reference 1 treats the free-jazz/modal boundary as dispositive and votes scope_call; Reference 2 judges Karma's bridge function and exceptional consensus sufficient to override the newly opened-gate default and votes consensus_core. Both agree on must_have priority and on the album's extraordinary spiritual-jazz stature.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes that John make an explicit free-jazz/modal scope ruling on Karma, with its exceptional consensus and bridge value strongly favoring it if he finds the record's ecstatic language compatible with the canon.
